sections.body_en:
Since the Sages forbade eating meat with milk even when they were not cooked together, one who eats dairy foods and wishes to eat meat afterwards must remove the remnants of milk from his mouth by wiping (kinu'aḥ) and rinsing (hadaḥa) the mouth, and only afterwards may he eat meat. The wiping is done by eating a firm food such as bread or fruit, and the rinsing by drinking. But one should not wipe the mouth by eating flour, dates or leafy vegetables, because they stick to the teeth and do not properly wipe away the remnants of the previous food (Ḥullin 104b; SA YD 89:2). Brushing the teeth and rinsing the mouth in the usual manner are effective in place of wiping and rinsing, and are even preferable to them, because they clean the mouth more of the remnants of milk.

In addition to wiping and rinsing the mouth, before eating the meat one must look at one's fingers, and if dairy grease is stuck to them – one must wash them (Ḥullin ibid.; SA ibid.).1

When one wishes to switch in the middle of a meal from dairy foods to meat foods, as many are accustomed to do on the holiday of Shavu'ot, in addition to wiping and rinsing the mouth and checking the fingers, one must clear away the dairy foods and their utensils and clean the table or change the tablecloth, and only afterwards serve the meat (Peninei Halakha, Mo'adim 13:14).2

notes_en.en:
The purpose of the wiping and rinsing is to remove remnants of milk and its taste that are stuck in the mouth, on the gums and on the teeth. Le-khatḥila one should chew the food well and pass the drink through the whole mouth, as is implied by the wording of SA 89:2: "and he should wipe his mouth well with it"; however, even with ordinary eating and drinking one fulfils the requirement of wiping and rinsing. Some say that one must swallow the food and the drink in order to wipe the throat (Pri Toar 7). And according to most poskim there is no need to swallow (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 9:26, Pri Megadim, Yad Yehuda), because the main thing is to wipe the area of the gums. That is why flour and dates are not effective. Therefore, instead of wiping and rinsing, one may brush one's teeth with a toothbrush and rinse the mouth. This is preferable to wiping and rinsing with foods, because when it is possible, it is better not to use foods for the purpose of wiping and cleaning, and it is also not befitting a person's dignity to eat for any purpose other than health and enjoyment. One does not wipe with vegetables (Ḥullin 105a), and the intention is leafy vegetables, which stick to the gums (Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 40:8).
In SA 89:2 it was ruled, following the Rambam, Ramban and Ran, that the law of wiping and rinsing applies only between milk and the meat of domesticated or wild animals, but for fowl it is not necessary. However, many are accustomed to be stringent with fowl as well, and so the Yad Yehuda explained the Rema, and so wrote the Knesset Ha-gedola, Shulḥan Gavoha, Zivḥei Tzedek and Ben Ish Ḥai (Year 2, Shelaḥ 14). And although one who wishes to be lenient may do so, le-khatḥila it is good not to multiply distinctions and to equate the laws of fowl with those of domesticated animals, and this is how I ruled without qualification above.

Some are meticulous to recite a berakha aḥarona (concluding blessing) and to wait an hour between eating milk and meat, so that eating the meat will be considered an entirely separate eating (Shelah and Pri Ḥadash 89:6, based on the Zohar 2:125a). However, in practice there is no need to be stringent in this, and immediately after eating milk one may wipe and rinse the mouth, check the hands and eat meat, in accordance with the words of SA 89:2; MB 494:16, and nearly all the poskim. The same law applies after yellow cheese (below, halakha 6). And if an hour has passed between eating the milk and the meat, there is no need to wipe and rinse the mouth and check the fingers, since presumably the milk remnants have dissolved and disappeared. And some say that the same law applies after half an hour. One who feels that even after an hour milk remnants still remain in his mouth should wipe and rinse his mouth before eating the meat.

sections.body_en:
Although after eating milk one may wipe and rinse the mouth and eat meat, after eating meat it is forbidden to eat milk, because the digestion of meat is prolonged and its taste is strong and lasts for a long time, and one who eats milk after meat may sense the taste of meat and milk together. Furthermore, meat is firm and may become stuck between the teeth, and only after a time is it released from the teeth or does its taste dissipate. However, the Talmud does not explain how long one must wait between eating meat and milk; only the words of Mar Ukva, who was one of the early Amora'im, are cited, who testified about himself that in this matter he was like vinegar compared to wine, for his father was stringent to wait twenty-four hours between eating meat and milk, whereas he sufficed with waiting until the next meal (Ḥullin 105a).

According to most Rishonim, Mar Ukva's intention was to teach us that one must interrupt between eating meat and eating milk for at least the length of time between the two meals that people were accustomed to eat every day, the first in the morning and the second in the evening (Rabbeinu Ḥananel and Rif). When they calculated the hours, it emerged that at least six hours passed between the two meals, for even those who ate their morning meal late, towards midday, waited at least six hours until the evening meal, which was after the Arvit prayer. It follows that the time one must wait between eating meat and milk is six hours (Rambam, Ittur, Rosh, Rashba, Ran and Gra). And this is the practice of those of Sephardic descent and most of those of Ashkenazic descent (SA and Rema 89:1).

And according to some of the great early Ashkenazic Rishonim, what is learned from Mar Ukva's words is that it is forbidden to eat meat and milk at the same meal, but at the following meal, no matter when it takes place, it is permitted to eat milk. Therefore, immediately after finishing the meat meal and Birkat Ha-mazon, one may clean the table, wipe and rinse the mouth, and eat a dairy meal (Tosafot, Ra'avya). The holders of this opinion were accustomed to wait at least an hour between eating the meat and eating the milk, so that through this it is clearly evident that they are two separate meals. And since one waits an hour, there is no longer any need to be careful about wiping and rinsing the mouth, and only if it is known that meat remnants remain between the teeth must one remove them beforehand. And this is the practice of some of those of Ashkenazic descent (Rema 89:1; Shakh 7). And some of those of Ashkenazic descent are accustomed to wait three hours between eating meat and milk, and their reasoning is that since people began to eat three meals a day, this is the shortest time that people customarily leave between meals.

Many of the later Ashkenazic poskim encouraged everyone to wait six hours between meat and milk (Rema 89:1; Shakh 8). However, it seems in practice that since the basis of this halakha is rabbinic, and it is proper to respect the customs of Israel that were founded by great Torah scholars, one should not persuade those who are accustomed to be lenient and wait one hour or three hours to change their custom. But anyone whose family has no clear custom to be lenient should take care to keep six hours, in accordance with the custom of most of Israel.3

notes_en.en:
Ḥullin 105a: "Rav Ḥisda said: If one ate meat – it is forbidden to eat cheese; cheese – it is permitted to eat meat… Mar Ukva said: I, in this matter, am vinegar the son of wine compared to my father, for my father – when he would eat meat now – would not eat cheese until this time tomorrow, whereas I – at this meal I do not eat, at another meal – I eat." According to the Behag, She'iltot, Razah, Rabbeinu Tam and Ra'ah, even at the same meal one may eat milk after meat, after wiping and rinsing the mouth. And the fact that Mar Ukva would wait the length of time from meal to meal is because he did not wipe his mouth (Razah), or because he followed a pious practice (Rabbeinu Tam). I did not mention this opinion above, because no one practises in accordance with it.
Tosafot and the Ra'avya hold that according to Mar Ukva's words it is permitted to eat milk only at the next meal; however, the Sages did not distinguish between whether a long or a short time passes between them – as long as it is at a different meal, it is permitted to eat milk. Therefore, immediately after finishing a meat meal, one may recite the blessing, clear the table, wipe and rinse the mouth and begin a dairy meal. However, some say that one should not recite a berakha aḥarona in order to begin a new meal immediately, because it is an unnecessary blessing. And people were accustomed to wait an hour between the meals (Hagahot Sha'arei Dura by the author of Terumat Ha-deshen; Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 40:3; Maharil). And so it is written in the Zohar (2:125b), that one should not eat meat and milk in one hour and at one meal.
And according to most Rishonim, one must wait the length of time customary between one meal and the next, because this is what we learned from Mar Ukva, that although he was not as stringent with himself as his father, he was careful not to eat milk until the next meal (Rabbeinu Ḥananel and Rif). And since people were accustomed to eat two meals a day, one must wait according to the time between them. The Sages said (Shabbat 10a) that in the third hour of the day heirs (who do not need to work) would eat, in the fourth most people, in the fifth labourers, and in the sixth Torah scholars. It follows that those who ate late could finish their meal at the end of the sixth hour, and the evening meal was after the twelfth hour; it follows that even for the latest, at least six hours passed between the two meals (Leḥem Mishneh and Gra). And so wrote the Rambam, Rashba, Rosh, Ittur, Ran and others, that one must wait about six hours. And so it was ruled in SA 89:1. And so they practised in the lands of the East and North Africa, except for a few in North Africa who were lenient with three hours.
The Ashkenazic custom: in the period of the Rishonim and until about five hundred years ago, people were accustomed to wait one hour; however, together with the migration to Eastern Europe and the establishment of the new communities in Poland, the custom of waiting six hours, in accordance with the words of most Rishonim, began to spread. The Rema wrote (89:1): "And the simple custom in these countries is to wait one hour after eating meat, and afterwards to eat cheese… And some are meticulous to wait six hours after eating meat before cheese, and so it is proper to do." And some urged everyone to be stringent, as the Maharshal and Shakh 89:8 wrote, that anyone "who has a scent of Torah" should wait six hours. About a hundred and fifty years ago this custom had already become binding in Eastern Europe, to the point that the Arukh Ha-shulḥan wrote (89:7): "And so is the simple custom in all the dispersions of Israel, to wait six hours, and heaven forbid to change it, and of this it is said 'one who breaches a fence,' etc."
However, in Western Europe many were accustomed to wait only an hour. And some of the people of Western Europe accepted in principle the opinion of most Rishonim that one must wait the length of time between two meals; however, since they were accustomed to eat three meals a day, they were accustomed to wait three hours, which is the shortest waiting time between two meals (see Darkhei Teshuva 89:6). Since the basis of this law is rabbinic, and the lenient position follows the opinion of some of the great Rishonim, and there is value in preserving customs whose foundation is firm, it is not proper to encourage those who are accustomed to be lenient to change their custom. And in my humble opinion, even the Aḥaronim who ruled emphatically that those of Ashkenazic descent should wait six hours intended the people of their own region in Eastern Europe, and not the people of Western Europe, whose clear custom was to be lenient.
When there is a difference between the customs of the husband's and the wife's families, it is proper for the wife to follow the custom of her husband's family, as we learned in the Torah regarding the wife of a kohen, who eats teruma like him.
Fowl: In the Gemara (Ḥullin 104b), an opinion is cited according to which: "Fowl and cheese may be eaten freely (be-apikoren)… without washing the hands and without wiping the mouth." Some Rishonim learned from this that although after eating meat one must wait six hours (as from meal to meal), after eating fowl one may immediately eat cheese (Ramban, Ritva). And some are accustomed to wait six hours after meat, and after fowl one hour, or three, or four. And as we learned, every person may continue the custom of his forefathers. However, according to the Rambam (9:28) and Rashba, the halakha does not follow this opinion, and even after fowl one must wait six hours, and so it was ruled in the SA (89:1), and this is the opinion of nearly all the Aḥaronim. Apparently, since the Sages established a prohibition on fowl meat with milk like the meat of domesticated animals, they did not wish to distinguish in the details of their laws.

sections.body_en:
As we learned, the prevalent custom is to wait six hours between eating meat and eating milk, but there is no need to wait six hours from the end of the meat meal until the beginning of the dairy meal (Dagul Me-revava 89:1).

Some hold that the intention of the Rishonim was not to wait six full hours, since they had no clocks, and it is reasonable that they did not require precision in this; rather, once more than five hours have passed and the sixth hour has already begun, it is permitted to eat milk. And some say that after five and a half hours it is permitted to eat milk, since most of the sixth hour has already passed. And according to many of the Aḥaronim, one must be precise that six full hours pass. And so it seems, because since clocks became widespread and the daily schedule is set according to precise times, even the words of the Rishonim who said to wait about six hours must be fulfilled precisely. Beyond that, we have learned that in practice most people were accustomed to wait about eight hours between the meals (Shabbat 10a), and even one who ate the morning meal late waited about six hours or more until the evening meal; consequently, one should not be lenient with less than six hours.

However, when necessary one may be lenient after five and a half hours, and in a pressing situation one may be lenient even after more than five hours have passed. And one who wishes to be lenient le-khatḥila after more than five hours has a basis on which to rely. And those who are meticulous are stringent to wait six full hours even in a pressing situation.4

notes_en.en:
Some of the Rishonim wrote "like six hours" (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 9:28; Kol Bo), and some wrote "about six hours" (Rashba). Some learn from this that it suffices for more than five hours to pass, as the Meiri wrote (Ḥullin 105a): "six hours or close to it," and elsewhere (Magen Avot 9:47): "five or six hours." And it was testified that this was the practice in the yeshivot in Lithuania, and so wrote the Melumdei Milḥama 104. And some say that the expression "about six hours" means close to six, that is, that more than five and a half hours have passed, and it is likewise known that anything "close" is less than half an hour (see Yabi'a Omer, YD 1:4). And some say that in winter, when the interval between meals is shorter, one may wait about four hours (Pri Ḥadash 89:6), and some say that when the meat meal is during the day and the dairy meal at night, one may suffice with waiting more than five hours. And some say that if one slept between the meat meal and the dairy meal, one may suffice with four or five hours (Da'at Kedoshim 89:2). And some say that the reason six full hours are not required is that the mealtime of Torah scholars who were engaged in judging could begin at the end of the sixth hour and continue until the end of the seventh hour, so that in practice less than six hours passed until the time of the evening meal (Derisha ḤM 5:7). However, on the other hand, most Torah scholars ate within the sixth hour, whereas the evening meal was after the Arvit prayer, that is, in the middle of the first hour of the night; thus in practice they interrupted about seven hours between the meals, and only in winter, when the day is short, did it turn out that they waited six hours, and all the rest of the public would wait, even in winter, at least eight hours.
In the Tur and Shulḥan Arukh (89:1) it was ruled: "six hours," implying no less, and so wrote most of the later poskim. One may say that when clocks were not common, the requirement was to wait at least about six hours according to the person's estimate, and as clocks became more common and the arrangements of life are set according to precise hours, the halakha too must be defined precisely, and consequently the ruling is to wait six full hours. Nevertheless, since there are lenient opinions, when necessary one may be lenient after five and a half hours have passed, and in a pressing situation after five hours. And one who wishes to be lenient in this always has a basis on which to rely, in combination with the opinion of those who hold that it suffices to wait one hour or three hours. And many are careful always to wait six hours. Similarly, in educational institutions, when waiting six hours disrupts the institution's schedule, some hold that one should not be lenient with less than six hours (Rav Eliyahu, Ma'amar Mordekhai 2, YD 4), and many are accustomed to be lenient and keep only most of the sixth hour.
In a situation of doubt whether six hours have passed, even those who are meticulous to wait six hours may be lenient and eat milk. Admittedly, some say that since it is a "davar she-yesh lo matirin," that is, something that is about to become permitted on its own, one should wait until one is out of the doubt (Yad Yehuda 89:1); however, on the other hand, since it is a rabbinic law whose basis is custom, and some are lenient le-khatḥila after an hour, and some are lenient le-khatḥila after more than five hours, in a case of doubt one may be lenient le-khatḥila. Furthermore, some say that the concept of "davar she-yesh lo matirin" cannot be applied to time, since time that has passed will not return (Darkhei Teshuva 89:5).

sections.title_en: The Reason for the Prohibition and the Details of the Laws
sections.body_en:
Two main reasons were given for waiting between eating meat and milk. 1) The taste of meat is strong and may be sensed for up to six hours (Rashi). 2) Meat is firm, and pieces of it may become stuck between the teeth, and after six hours have passed they are already released or their taste has dissipated (Rambam). In practice we take both reasons into account, and therefore even one who chewed meat for a baby must wait six hours, since in chewing, the meat can become stuck between the teeth. And even one who ate soft meat must wait six hours, because of its taste, which can remain for up to six hours (Tur 89:1).

One who ate meat and after a time found meat stuck in his teeth should remove it from his mouth, in order to maintain the separation of six hours between the meat and the milk. Be-di'avad, if he swallowed it, he has not lost the count of six hours, because there is no need to be concerned about the taste lingering from it. And if he found the meat after six hours and wishes to eat milk immediately, after removing it from his mouth he should clean his mouth by wiping and rinsing or by brushing his teeth (as explained above, halakha 1), and immediately afterwards he may eat milk. Be-di'avad, even if he swallowed the meat, he may clean his mouth and afterwards immediately eat milk (Rema 89:1; Shakh 3-4).5

notes_en.en:
Be-di'avad, if one swallowed meat that was stuck between his teeth, he does not need to wait six hours from swallowing it, because the taste of the meat dissipates over time, and according to the Rambam (according to the Tur), if after six hours meat remains in one's teeth, there is no prohibition in it, because its taste has already dissipated through the fluids in the mouth. And even if we say that according to Rashi its taste does not dissipate, be-di'avad one may rely on the Rambam, especially since perhaps even according to Rashi, after one has already waited six hours there is no need to be concerned about the taste lingering from such a small piece. And one may add the positions of the Rishonim who suffice with wiping (above, note 3). Moreover, several poskim ruled that even one who has holes and cracks in his teeth, in which pieces of meat may become stuck, is not obligated to clean them with a toothpick (Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥullin 105a). Admittedly, according to many poskim he must clean them with a toothpick (Yam Shel Shlomo, Ḥullin 8:9; Ben Ish Ḥai, Year 2, Shelaḥ 8). But it seems that be-di'avad, even according to them, one who has no toothpick to pick his teeth may eat milk after six hours.
If one erred and recited a blessing over a dairy food before six hours had passed: if he had managed to wipe his mouth with food and drink after eating the meat, or had already finished the meal, or an hour had passed – since there are Rishonim who hold that in such a case it is permitted, in order that he not sin with a berakha le-vatala (a blessing in vain), he should rely on them and eat a little after the blessing (Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 12:11; and see Yabi'a Omer 2, YD 5; Badei Ha-shulḥan 89:1, s.v. "ve-yesh medakdekim").

sections.title_en: A Meat Dish, and the Presumed Status of Meat or Dairy
sections.body_en:
It is customary that even one who eats a dish that was cooked with the meat of a domesticated animal or fowl, since the dish had a taste of meat, should not eat milk, or a dish that has a taste of milk, for six hours. Therefore, one who eats potatoes that were cooked with meat, or a clear soup that was cooked with meat, must wait six hours before eating potatoes that were cooked with milk (Beit Yosef OḤ 173:1; Rema YD 89:3).

A food that is "be-ḥezkat besari" (presumed to be meaty), even though the taste of meat is not sensed in it, is forbidden to be eaten with milk, but immediately after finishing eating it, it is permitted to eat milk. For example, one who eats salads that were served at a meat meal, from which people also took with the cutlery with which they ate meat – the salads are considered be-ḥezkat besari, and therefore it is forbidden to eat them with dairy foods (above 25:7, note 7). But since a taste of meat is not sensed in them, it is permitted at the same meal, immediately after eating them, to eat milk. Likewise, when one fries in the same oil once meat and once falafel balls, as long as the falafel balls have no taste of meat, they are only be-ḥezkat besari, and it is forbidden to eat them with milk, but there is no need to wait six hours after them.

This is the rule: anything that is be-ḥezkat besari but in which a taste of meat is not sensed is forbidden to be eaten with milk, and after eating it, it is permitted to eat milk. Likewise, after eating meat it is permitted to eat a food that is "be-ḥezkat ḥalavi" (presumed to be dairy), as long as the taste of milk is not sensed in it.6

notes_en.en: According to the law, there is no need to wait after eating a dish that has a taste of meat, for we learned (Ḥullin 105b) that it is obligatory to wash the hands between eating a meat dish and milk, but there is no need to wait at all (Rabbeinu Tam, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, Rashba, Rosh, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Ritva, Tur and SA 89:3). Indeed, the reasons given for waiting do not apply to a meat dish, for the concern that meat will remain between the teeth applies specifically to actual meat and not to its taste, and also the strong taste of meat lasts a long time specifically after eating meat and not after a meat dish. However, several Rishonim wrote that in practice people are accustomed to be stringent and wait (Mordekhai, Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 40:2). And so it is cited in the Beit Yosef OḤ 173:1, and Rema 89:3. And this is agreed upon by all the Aḥaronim (Ḥida, Zivḥei Tzedek). But if falafel balls were afterwards fried in oil in which meat had been fried, the falafel balls are not considered a meat dish. Because whenever the meat is not a main component of the dish, the dish is not considered meaty (Baḥ, Shakh 89:19). Admittedly, there is room to be stringent when the meat remnants in the oil impart a clear taste to the falafel, but when a clear taste of meat is not sensed in the falafel, one should not be stringent. And so wrote the Yad Yehuda (89, Arokh 5). And there is no room to be stringent in this, since the whole discussion concerns a rabbinic prohibition, and according to the Razah and those who agree with him, even after eating actual meat it suffices to wipe the mouth, and even according to most Rishonim, who hold that one must wait six hours after eating meat, after a dish in which the taste of meat is very noticeable there is no need to wait at all. (And some hold that the law of nat bar nat applies to foods too, and in their opinion it is even permitted to eat with milk a food that received a taste of meat as nat bar nat; see Halikhot Olam 7, Koraḥ 12.)

sections.body_en:
Among the great Rishonim in Ashkenaz, there were those who were accustomed to be stringent and wait between eating hard cheese and meat just as one waits between eating a meat dish and milk, because the taste of this cheese is strong and lasts no less than that of a meat dish, and just as people are stringent to wait after a meat dish that contains no meat, so one should wait after eating hard cheese. Also, because the cheese is hard and pieces of it may become stuck between the teeth like meat. However, they ruled this in accordance with their custom of waiting one hour after eating meat, and consequently they also ruled to wait one hour after eating hard cheese. After many in Ashkenaz accepted the custom of waiting six hours between meat and milk, many of them were stringent to wait six hours between hard cheese and meat as well. However, their stringency concerned hard cheese that was prepared over the course of six months, or whose preparation process took less time but which was intensified by worms and mould that produced fermentation that greatly strengthened the taste of the cheese. And some went further and were stringent with any hard cheese, even if it was made over the course of a few days, such as yellow cheese, lest pieces of it become stuck in the teeth.

In practice, the halakha follows the opinion of most poskim, and there is no obligation to wait after hard cheese any more than after ordinary cheese. Those who wish to be meticulous should wait one hour between eating hard cheese and meat.7

notes_en.en: This stringent custom was practised only in Ashkenaz, as cited in the Issur Ve-heter He-arokh and Rema 89:2, perhaps because there people were accustomed to prepare such hard cheeses. They were stringent to wait one hour, as was the custom in Ashkenaz between meat and milk, as the Issur Ve-heter He-arokh (40:10) and the Shakh (89:16) wrote. However, in recent generations, just as people became stringent to wait six hours between meat and milk, according to this custom they became stringent to wait six hours after hard cheese (Taz 89:4; Pri Megadim, Siftei Da'at 16; Ḥokhmat Adam 40:13; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 494:15). And some even included yellow cheese in hard cheese (Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, Shevet Ha-levi 2:35). And many wrote that only after very hard cheese must one wait (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Rav Aharon Kotler, Hora'a Berura 89:33). Also among the Ashkenazic Aḥaronim, many wrote that even after very hard cheese there is no obligation to wait even an hour, and so many practise (Yam Shel Shlomo, Ḥullin 8:6; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 89:11; Igrot Moshe YD 2:26, and as most of the Ashkenazic Rishonim ruled without qualification). In the lands of the East and North Africa people were not accustomed to be stringent in this, and only in recent generations, in a few places, were there those who were accustomed to be stringent to wait three hours or six hours (see Ben Ish Ḥai, Year 2, Shelaḥ 15). In practice, since the basis of waiting between meat and milk is rabbinic, and the waiting between hard cheese and meat derives from a stringent custom written by some Rishonim, and even they intended to wait only one hour, and only after very hard cheese whose method of production is special, even those who are stringent should not be more stringent than that. And even one who wishes to be more meticulous should be stringent with very hard cheese for six hours, but not with yellow cheese, after which one may immediately eat meat with wiping and rinsing. And if he waits an hour, he will not even need wiping and rinsing, and only if he feels that its taste is stuck in his mouth should he brush his teeth or wipe and rinse his mouth.

sections.body_en:
The Torah forbade feeding forbidden foods to children and babies. Anyone who places forbidden food in the hand of a minor is considered as feeding him and thereby transgresses a Torah prohibition, for this is the usual way of feeding a minor (Yevamot 114a; Shabbat 90b). In addition, parents are commanded to educate their child to fulfil the mitzvot, and therefore parents who see their child eating forbidden food on his own must separate him from it (Rambam; SA OḤ 343:1).8

Likewise, there is a mitzva to educate the children to wait between eating meat and milk. In principle, one should educate them in this from when they understand the mitzva and are able to calculate the hours one must wait between meat and milk. However, it is a well-known rule that one does not educate children in a way that may cause them distress or harm their health. For this reason, one does not educate minors aged seven and eight to fast a number of hours on Yom Kippur (Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 9:8).

Based on these rules, we will describe the process of education towards observing the interval between meat and milk. Babies who do not yet understand the difference between meat and milk – it is permitted to feed them milk after meat, provided that their mouths and hands are cleaned of meat remnants, so that they will not be fed meat and milk together. When small children begin to understand the difference between meat and milk, but have not yet reached the age at which they are able to distinguish between long and short times, roughly between the ages of three and five, it is proper, when possible, that they wait about an hour between meat and milk. And when it is necessary to give them milk so that they will go to sleep, or so that they will not cry, one may rinse their mouths and hands and give them milk without waiting an hour.

From when they reach the age at which they are able to distinguish somewhat between times, around the age of five or six, one must begin to accustom them to interrupt between eating meat and milk. And since very often the time of their next meal is before six hours have passed since eating the meat, one may suffice with accustoming them to wait about three hours.

From when they reach the age of nine or ten, since they already know how to calculate the hours and are able to wait longer between meals, it is proper, when possible, to accustom them to wait about six hours. When necessary, for example when they are eating with their younger siblings and it is difficult to feed them afterwards, they may wait only three hours between the meals. And only about a year before they reach the age of mitzvot should they become accustomed to wait six hours.9

notes_en.en: In Yevamot 114a it is explained that it is forbidden by Torah law to feed a minor something forbidden, such as sheratzim (creeping creatures), and in the Mishna and Gemara Shabbat 90b it is explained that already by placing the food in the minor's hands one transgresses the prohibition. And so it is explained in MB 343:4. In addition, by virtue of the mitzva of education, one must separate a minor who comes to eat forbidden things on his own. There is a difficulty, for they said in Yevamot 113b-114a: "A minor who eats nevelot (carcasses) – the court is not commanded to separate him." According to the Rambam, most Rishonim and SA OḤ 343:1, only the parents are obligated in the education of their child, which includes separating him from eating forbidden food, but the court and other people are not commanded to separate him. And some hold that the law of the father, the court and other people is the same, and what they said, that one is not obligated to separate a minor, refers to a minor who has not reached the age of education; but a minor who has reached the age of education – the parents and anyone who can help in his education are commanded to separate him from the prohibition (Tosafot, Rosh and Ritva). The Rema mentioned them as the opinion of "some say." And the Ḥayei Adam (66:3) and MB (343:7) wrote that with a Torah prohibition it is proper for others to be stringent and separate him. And see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 24:3, and in the Harḥavot there, 24:3:6-7.

The mitzva of education begins from when the child is able to understand how the mitzva is fulfilled (see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 24:1). It follows that in this law, from when the child knows how to distinguish between meat and milk and knows how to calculate the six hours, there is a mitzva to educate him to be careful in this. However, when this carefulness may disrupt the arrangement of his meals and consequently his health, there is no obligation to educate him in it, just as we find that there is no mitzva to educate minors aged eight to fast even a few hours on Yom Kippur (Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 9:8). And one cannot argue that according to those who hold that one must wait six hours, one who gives milk to minors before then is considered as feeding them a prohibition (the prohibition of "sefiya," as explained in Yevamot 114a). For the Hagahot Maimoniyot (Shabbat 29:40) wrote, regarding eating before Kiddush, that since the food has no intrinsic prohibition, but the prohibition is only on account of the time, there is no prohibition of "sefiya" in it, and this opinion is taken into account in the halakha (cited in Beit Yosef OḤ 269; see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 6:9), and the same law applies to eating milk after meat. Not only that, but according to the Rashba and Ran, when it is needed for a minor, it is permitted to feed him a rabbinic prohibition. And although according to most poskim it is forbidden, and only in a pressing situation does one rely on the Rashba and Ran (see Harḥavot to Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 24:5:1-2), here, where some hold that from the outset it is permitted to eat milk after one hour, one may be lenient when necessary for any minor, until close to the age of mitzvot, to wait only one hour.
To summarise: there is a mitzva to educate the minor to wait between meat and milk, and over the years to progress until he keeps six hours (for the majority of Israel, who practise so). And since this is a process that depends on many factors, this law contains a general direction, which should be applied flexibly according to the situation. First, one must take into account the physical and emotional state of the child, for a healthy child is not like a weak one, nor a brave child like a pampered one. The mitzva of education also depends on the character of the parents, for every parent is commanded to educate according to his character, and some tend towards strictness and some towards leniency. The mitzva also depends on the arrangements of the home, for if there are small children there, the meals are closer together, and there is more need to be lenient. Therefore, it is not possible to set clear boundaries, but only directions in principle, and that is why the halakha was formulated in the language of "proper" and "fitting." Likewise we find general guidance in most poskim, and among those who went into detail, different guidance was given, which stems mainly from the difference in patterns of life. It should be added that in the order of progress it is proper to take the opinions of the poskim into account: when possible, one keeps an hour; when possible, one keeps three hours; and when possible, six hours.

sections.body_en:
Any forbidden food that is needed for the recovery of a person who is dangerously ill is permitted, for pikuaḥ nefesh (saving a life) overrides all the mitzvot of the Torah. But a sick person whose illness is not dangerous is forbidden to eat forbidden foods.

However, regarding the accepted custom of waiting six hours, if the sick person needs to eat milk after meat, he may suffice with waiting one hour, and he should take care to brush his teeth and rinse his mouth beforehand (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 89:7; and see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 24, note 4).

sections.title_en: A Reason for the Prohibition of Meat and Milk
sections.body_en:
The mitzvot of the Torah are divided into two types, mishpatim and ḥukim. The mishpatim are mitzvot whose reason is understood by man, and even without the divine command man could have arrived at them through the intellect that God granted him, such as the mitzvot between man and his fellow, and the mitzvot dealing with faith, such as prayer and tefillin. In contrast, the ḥukim are mitzvot whose reason is beyond human comprehension, such as the prohibition of meat and milk, which we merited to receive only through the prophetic revelation of the Torah (Rambam, Hilkhot Me'ila 8:8). Nevertheless, even from the ḥukim one can receive inspiration for profound ideas, which are also included in the mitzva of Torah study. Some explained that this prohibition is intended to restrain desire and cruelty, for it is not proper to be cruel to animals and take both their milk and their meat and cook them together, similar to the prohibition of eating an animal and its offspring on one day (Rashbam and Ibn Ezra, Shemot 23:19; Ramban, Devarim 14:21; Rav Kook, Ḥazon Ha-tzimḥonut Ve-ha-shalom 14).

The commentators further wrote that the prohibition of meat and milk is included among the prohibitions of kilayim (forbidden mixtures), which are intended to preserve the uniqueness of each species, so as not to blur it by mixing it with another species (Ḥinukh 92; Rabbeinu Baḥya and Rav S.R. Hirsch on Shemot 23:19; see above 3:1).

The prohibition of meat and milk has an added stringency, in that it is forbidden even for benefit, similar to the stringency of kilei ha-kerem, which are forbidden for benefit (see above 5:5). Indeed, the difference between meat and milk is striking. Meat is an important food whose preparation as kosher is complex and complicated. It must be of a kosher species, it must be slaughtered according to halakha, checked for tereifot, and cleansed of blood, ḥelev (forbidden fat) and forbidden sinews. Even after it has been made kosher from a halakhic standpoint, its preparation for eating involves cooking or roasting, and even eating it, chewing it and digesting it are heavy. In contrast, milk is a light and simple food, and in the pure species it is kosher by its nature, and drinking it is easy. Likewise, preparing and eating cheese is easier than preparing and eating meat. Meat is a food of adults, whereas milk is a food of babies and children.

Meat comes into being through birth, and consequently it expresses a new stage of life, whereas milk is produced in order to make life that already exists grow. Meat expresses vitality at a higher level, for it was actually a living creature, whereas milk expresses vitality at a lower level. One may therefore say that meat expresses existential and great values and considerations, whereas milk expresses small and light values and considerations. Each is right and proper in its place, but one who mixes them sins by mixing values and considerations of different orders of magnitude, and thereby destroys the order of life and distorts the moral compass. And since this matter is so important and so dangerous, it is understandable why the Sages added many fences around the prohibition of cooking meat in milk (Likutei Halakhot by Rabbi Natan, Basar Be-ḥalav 5).10

notes_en.en:
For example, the freedom of every person is very important, but when the economic reality is so difficult that many people cannot survive without the institution of slavery, the Torah preferred the existential consideration and gave a place to the institution of slavery, while infringing on people's freedom. Until humanity reaches the stage at which people will be able to survive without slavery, and then slavery will be forbidden.
Similarly, when a couple who meet with a view to marriage find themselves suited in terms of character traits and shared values, and discover that there is love between them, but something in the young woman's appearance does not quite find favour in the young man's eyes, and something in the young man's manner of speaking does not quite find favour in the young woman's eyes – they must avoid giving equal weight to small and great considerations. And so it is in choosing a profession and a place of residence and everything in life. That is, although every consideration has value, one who mixes considerations of different orders of magnitude with one another destroys his ability to make a moral and successful choice and causes himself enormous harm.
